content: Urinary tract infections (UTIs), including pyelonephritis, are significant complications during pregnancy that can result in serious maternal and neonatal health issues, including morbidity and mortality. A wide range of antibiotics and combinations of these drugs are available for treating UTIs, but most have been tested in non-pregnant populations. This makes it challenging to determine the optimal antibiotic regimen for pregnant women. The purpose of this review was to identify, using the best available evidence from randomized controlled trials, which antibiotic is most effective for treating symptomatic UTIs during pregnancy. The outcomes assessed included cure rates, recurrence of infection, preterm delivery, premature rupture of membranes, neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) admissions, the need to switch antibiotics, and the occurrence of prolonged fever. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group Trials Register (as of November 2009) and reviewed reference lists of relevant articles. They included trials that randomly assigned pregnant participants to at least two different treatment options for symptomatic UTIs. The quality of the trials was assessed, and data were extracted by the review authors. A total of 10 studies involving 1,125 pregnant women were included in the analysis. In most comparisons, there were no significant differences between the treatments in terms of cure rates, recurrence of infection, preterm delivery, NICU admissions, the need to change antibiotics, or prolonged fever. However, when cefuroxime was compared to cephradine, the cefuroxime group showed better cure rates (29 out of 49 versus 41 out of 52) and fewer recurrences (20 out of 49 versus 11 out of 52). Another notable finding was that women treated as outpatients had a longer gestational age at birth (38.86 weeks versus 37.21 weeks), while infants born to women treated as inpatients had a higher average birth weight (3,120 grams versus 2,659 grams). The authors concluded that while antibiotic treatment is effective in curing UTIs during pregnancy, there is insufficient evidence to recommend a specific drug regimen. All the antibiotics studied were highly effective in reducing adverse outcomes, and complications were rare. However, the small sample sizes of the included trials limit the ability to detect meaningful differences between treatments. Future research should focus on identifying the most promising antibiotics by evaluating factors such as drug class, timing, dosage, acceptability, maternal and neonatal outcomes, and cost.
